gloss: Growth that is too thick, too fast, or where it is not wanted.
examples: The path behind the shed disappeared under *overgrowth*.
Antibiotics can lead to bacterial *overgrowth* in the gut.
We spent Saturday cutting back the *overgrowth* along the fence.

gloss: The condition of becoming dangerously or harmfully hot.
examples: The laptop shut itself down to prevent *overheating*.
*Overheating* is a common problem with these older engines.
Economists warned about *overheating* in the housing market.

gloss: Much more of something than the situation actually needs.
examples: Three cameras for one small room is *overkill*.
The security at the concert felt like *overkill*.
A little garlic is fine, but a whole head is *overkill*.

gloss: A part where two things cover, share, or coincide with each other.
examples: There's a big *overlap* between the two job descriptions.
The shingles are laid with a two-inch *overlap*.
The auditors found several *overlaps* in the two budgets.
contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable (OH-vur-lap); the verb stresses the last (oh-vur-LAP).

gloss: A layer or sheet placed on top of something else.
examples: The map has a plastic *overlay* showing the bus routes.
She added a text *overlay* to the video.
The app uses colored *overlays* to mark flood zones.
contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable (OH-vur-lay); the verb stresses the last (oh-vur-LAY).

gloss: A ruler who holds power over other rulers or over a whole territory.
examples: The villagers paid a share of every harvest to their *overlord*.
In the game you play a dark *overlord* building an army.
The colony's *overlords* lived thousands of miles away.

gloss: An amount of money paid that is more than what was owed.
examples: The state asked her to return the *overpayment*.
We found an *overpayment* of about two hundred dollars.
The audit turned up dozens of small *overpayments*.

gloss: A response that is far stronger than the situation calls for.
examples: Canceling the whole trip over one bad review is an *overreaction*.
His anger seemed like an *overreaction* to me.
The market's *overreactions* usually correct within a week.

gloss: Someone who watches over workers and makes sure the work gets done.
examples: The plantation *overseer* kept a log of every shipment.
She works as an *overseer* on the night shift.
The *overseers* reported directly to the owner.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A mistake caused by not noticing something, or the work of supervising something.
examples: Leaving your name off the list was an *oversight*, not an insult.
Congress has *oversight* of the agency's budget.
A few small *oversights* delayed the whole project.
contrast: Countable it means an error; uncountable it means supervision — opposite feelings from one word.

gloss: The removal of a government or ruler by force.
examples: The book describes the *overthrow* of the king in a single night.
Protesters called for the *overthrow* of the regime.
The region has seen three violent *overthrows* in twenty years.
contrast: The noun stresses the first syllable (OH-vur-throh); the verb stresses the last (oh-vur-THROH).

gloss: An extra meaning or feeling suggested by something without being said directly.
examples: The speech had clear political *overtones*.
There was an *overtone* of anger in her voice.
The film's religious *overtones* upset some viewers.

gloss: A short description of the main points of something.
examples: The first chapter gives an *overview* of the whole method.
Can you send me a one-page *overview* before the meeting?
The website has *overviews* of every department.

gloss: Too much work, or the exhaustion that comes from it.
examples: He collapsed from *overwork* in his second year of residency.
*Overwork* and poor sleep finally caught up with her.
The union blames *overwork* for the rise in accidents.

gloss: The release of an egg from a woman's ovary.
examples: The app tracks *ovulation* and predicts her fertile days.

gloss: A U-shaped bend in a river, or the curved lake left when the river cuts a new channel.
examples: The river makes a wide *oxbow* just past the bridge.

gloss: A small device that measures how much oxygen is in the blood.
examples: The nurse clipped an *oximeter* onto my finger.

gloss: The process of supplying something, especially blood or water, with oxygen.
examples: The monitor showed poor *oxygenation* overnight.
An aerator improves *oxygenation* in the fish tank.

gloss: A phrase that puts together two words with opposite meanings, like 'deafening silence'.

gloss: A hormone that starts labor and is linked to bonding and trust.

gloss: A small electronic device put in the chest to keep the heart beating steadily.

The *pacemaker* battery lasts about ten years.
Modern *pacemakers* can be checked over the phone.

gloss: The act of bringing a region or an angry group under control, often by force.

The report is sharply critical of the army's *pacification* campaign.

gloss: The belief that war and violence are always wrong.
examples: Her *pacifism* came out of her religious upbringing.
He went to prison for his *pacifism* during the war.
The group preaches strict *pacifism* in every situation.

gloss: Someone who refuses to take part in war or violence.

A group of *pacifists* marched to the capitol.

gloss: The speed at which a story, film, or activity moves along.

gloss: The work of putting things into boxes, or the material used to protect them.

gloss: A thick soft piece of material used for protection or cleaning, or a block of writing paper.

gloss: A flooded field where rice is grown.

gloss: Someone who follows an old nature-based or many-god religion rather than one of the major world faiths.

gloss: A game in which players shoot capsules of paint at each other with air guns.

gloss: Two things or people put together as a match.

gloss: A fabric pattern of curved teardrop shapes.

gloss: A word or phrase that reads the same forward and backward.

gloss: A fence of tall pointed stakes built for defense, or a line of steep cliffs.

gloss: A horse with a golden coat and a white mane and tail.

gloss: A small garden flower with wide flat petals, often in two colors.

gloss: All the gods of a religion taken together, or the group of the most admired people in a field.

gloss: A big cat such as a black leopard, or, in America, a cougar.

gloss: The office and authority of the pope, or the period during which one pope serves.

gloss: A boy who delivers newspapers to people's homes.

gloss: Someone who jumps from an aircraft using a parachute.

gloss: A statement or situation that contradicts itself but may still be true.

gloss: A perfect example of some quality.

The brochure calls the staff *paragons* of service.

gloss: A trained assistant who does legal work under a lawyer's supervision.

gloss: A similarity between two things, or a line of latitude on a map.

gloss: The use of matching grammatical structures in a sentence or list.

gloss: A value or limit that defines how something works or how far it can go.

gloss: A funny imitation of a serious work, person, or style.

gloss: A tendency to accept what happens without acting or resisting.

gloss: A master key that opens several locks, or a digital credential that signs you in without a password.

The novel describes the daily life of the *peasantry*.

gloss: A quick strike with a bird's beak, or a short light kiss.
examples: The hen gave my finger a sharp *peck*.
He gave her a *peck* on the cheek and left.
The birds took a few *pecks* at the feeder and flew off.

gloss: A substance found in fruit that makes jam and jelly set.
examples: Add *pectin* so the jam thickens properly.
Apples are naturally high in *pectin*.
The recipe calls for low-sugar *pectin*.

gloss: An odd or distinctive feature of someone or something.
examples: Every language has its *peculiarities*.
One *peculiarity* of the house is the door that opens onto nothing.
He's known for a few harmless *peculiarities*.

gloss: Someone who fusses far too much over small rules and details.
examples: Only a *pedant* would object to that comma.
He's a bit of a *pedant* about grammar.
*Pedants* filled the comment section within an hour.

gloss: Someone who travels around selling small goods, or who spreads something harmful.
examples: A *peddler* used to sell pots door to door.
The site is full of *peddlers* of bad medical advice.
Street *peddlers* line the boardwalk all summer.
contrast: American *peddler*; the British spelling *pedlar* is rare in the U.S.

gloss: The branch of medicine that treats children.
examples: She went into *pediatrics* after her residency.
*Pediatrics* is on the third floor.
The hospital is expanding its *pediatrics* department.
contrast: Ends in -s but takes a singular verb: *pediatrics* is, not are.

gloss: A small device that counts the number of steps you take.
examples: My *pedometer* says I walked six miles today.
The company handed out *pedometers* for a fitness challenge.
A phone works fine as a *pedometer*.

gloss: An adult who is sexually attracted to children.
examples: The guide explains how *pedophiles* approach children online.
He was convicted as a *pedophile* in 2009.
The registry lists convicted *pedophiles* by county.
contrast: American spelling *pedophile*; British *paedophile*.

gloss: Sexual attraction in an adult toward children.
examples: The documentary examines how the church handled *pedophilia*.
*Pedophilia* is a criminal offense in every state.
The report carefully distinguishes *pedophilia* from other offenses.

gloss: A quick or secret look at something.
examples: Take a *peek* in the oven and see if it's done.
She got a *peek* at the guest list.
No *peeks* until your birthday.
contrast: Sounds like *peak*, a mountain top, and *pique*, to annoy — three different words.

gloss: A game in which you hide your face and then show it again to make a baby laugh.
examples: She plays *peekaboo* with the baby for hours.
*Peekaboo* is the only trick that stops him crying.
He learned *peekaboo* before he could crawl.

gloss: Something that annoys you, most often in the phrase 'pet peeve'.
examples: Loud chewing is my biggest pet *peeve*.
Everyone in the office has a *peeve* about that printer.
The list of pet *peeves* got long fast.

gloss: A short pin or hook of wood, metal, or plastic used to hold or hang something.
examples: Hang your coat on the *peg* by the door.
The tent came with six aluminum *pegs*.
The shelf rests on four wooden *pegs*.

gloss: A board full of small holes that hooks fit into, used for hanging tools.
examples: His tools hang on a *pegboard* over the workbench.
We put up *pegboard* along one wall of the garage.
The hardware store displays keys on a *pegboard*.

gloss: An act done to show that you are sorry for something wrong.
examples: He did *penance* by washing every dish for a week.
The priest assigned a simple *penance*.
She treated the long drive as *penance*.

gloss: The act of getting into or through something, or how widely a product has spread in a market.
examples: The vest stopped the bullet's *penetration*.
Broadband *penetration* is still low in rural counties.
The report measures market *penetration* state by state.

gloss: An antibiotic made from mold, used against bacterial infections.
examples: He's allergic to *penicillin*.
The doctor prescribed *penicillin* for strep throat.
*Penicillin* changed medicine in the 1940s.

gloss: The male sex organ, also used for passing urine.
examples: The doctor examined his *penis* for a rash.
The class covers how the *penis* changes during puberty.
Pediatricians suggest using real words like *penis* with young children.
contrast: The plural is *penises*.

gloss: A state or federal prison for people serving long sentences.
examples: He served eight years in the state *penitentiary*.
The federal *penitentiary* sits just outside of town.
Two *penitentiaries* were closed last year.

gloss: A small folding knife you can carry in a pocket.
examples: He opened the box with a *penknife*.
A *penknife* won't get through airport security.
Grandpa collected old *penknives*.
contrast: The k is silent, and the plural changes f to v: *penknives*.

gloss: A triangular flag, especially one marking a league championship in baseball.
examples: A dusty *pennant* still hangs in his childhood bedroom.
The team won the *pennant* for the first time in decades.
Colored *pennants* were strung across the car lot.

gloss: Short tube-shaped pasta cut at an angle at both ends.
examples: Boil the *penne* for eleven minutes.
We had *penne* with vodka sauce.
*Penne* holds a thick sauce better than spaghetti does.
contrast: Two syllables, PEN-ay — not the same as *pen*.

gloss: Someone who lives on a pension after retiring.
examples: The bill would raise monthly payments for *pensioners*.
Most of the residents here are *pensioners*.
As a *pensioner*, he gets a discount on the bus.
contrast: Common in Britain; Americans more often say *retiree*.

gloss: A line of poetry made of five metrical feet, as in iambic pentameter.
examples: Shakespeare wrote most of his plays in iambic *pentameter*.
The class learned to hear *pentameter* by clapping it out.
The sonnet breaks out of *pentameter* in the last line.

gloss: An athletic contest made up of five different events.
examples: She won a bronze medal in the modern *pentathlon*.
The *pentathlon* includes fencing, swimming, and riding.
He has competed in three Olympic *pentathlons*.

gloss: A garden plant with large, full, sweet-smelling flowers in late spring.
examples: The *peonies* bloom right after the tulips.
She carried a bouquet of white *peonies*.
A single *peony* filled the whole room with scent.
contrast: The plural changes -y to -ies: *peonies*.

gloss: Lively energy and enthusiasm.
examples: The coach gave the team a *pep* talk at halftime.
There isn't much *pep* in the office on Mondays.
A cup of coffee put some *pep* in her step.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A strong-flavored mint plant and its oil, or a candy flavored with it.
examples: This tea tastes strongly of *peppermint*.
She keeps a bowl of *peppermints* by the register.
*Peppermint* oil is supposed to help with headaches.
contrast: Uncountable it means the plant or flavor; countable it means a single candy.

gloss: An enzyme in the stomach that breaks down protein.
examples: *Pepsin* starts digesting protein in the stomach.
The lab tested how *pepsin* works at different pH levels.
Without enough acid, *pepsin* cannot do its job.
